Illinois, 360 U.S. 264 (1959): https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/360/264 (the sentence continues "and, if it is in any way relevant to the case, the district attorney has the responsibility and duty to correct what he knows to be false and elicit the truth").

titre: Napue: the witness denies any promise, the prosecutor stays silent
accroche: Illinois, 1959: the key witness states that he was promised nothing. The prosecutor knows that is false, and says nothing. The Supreme Court overturns the conviction.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 21, 1938, four men walk into a dimly lit Chicago bar and announce a holdup. An off-duty police officer, who is in the room, opens fire. One of the robbers is killed, the officer is mortally wounded, and another robber, George Hamer, is seriously hit. Hamer pleads guilty to the officer's murder and receives 199 years in prison. An accomplice, Poe, is sentenced to death and executed. That leaves Henry Napue, arrested later.

## A witness playing for his sentence

At Napue's trial, the prosecution has little to go on: the passage of time and the poor light make identifications uncertain, and some witnesses have left the State. Hamer agrees to talk. According to the Supreme Court, his testimony makes up the bulk of the evidence.

On the stand, the assistant prosecutor asks him whether he received a promise in exchange for his testimony. Hamer answers no. That is false: the assistant had promised to recommend a reduction of his sentence. He says nothing. The jury learns only that a public defender had promised to "do what he could." Napue is sentenced to 199 years, like Hamer.

Later, that former assistant files a petition on Hamer's behalf, and writes in it that he had indeed made him that promise. Napue seizes on it. The Illinois Supreme Court acknowledges that the promise existed and that the assistant knew Hamer was lying, but refuses to overturn the conviction: the jury already knew that a public defender was trying to help the witness.

## A lie that is not about the crime

On June 15, 1959, the U.S. Supreme Court, in an opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren, overturns the conviction. It first recalls that a conviction obtained through false testimony that the State's representatives know to be false violates the Fourteenth Amendment. It adds that the result is the same when the State, without having solicited the lie, lets it pass uncorrected.

That leaves the State's objection: Hamer did not lie about the crime, only about his own interest in testifying. The Court answers that the assessment of a witness's truthfulness can decide guilt. It cites a decision of the New York Court of Appeals: "A lie is a lie, no matter what its subject." And it writes that, better informed, the jury might have concluded that Hamer was fabricating his account to win the favor of the State's representative running the case.

## The shift

False testimony is usually put on the witness's side. *Napue* moves the point of responsibility: whoever knows that a witness is lying, and keeps quiet, makes the trial as false as if he had asked for the lie. According to Wikipedia's article on the ruling, the Supreme Court will later refine this rule in *Giglio v. United States* (1972), extending it to the case where the prosecutor in the courtroom did not know, but his office did.

The Court does not say that Napue is innocent, or that Hamer lied about everything. It says only that the jury judged without knowing one of the witness's reasons for talking. How can we measure what the jury would have done with the truth?

repere.texte: On June 15, 1959, in Napue v. Illinois, the U.S. Supreme Court (opinion of Chief Justice Warren) holds that a conviction obtained through false testimony that the State knows to be false violates the Fourteenth Amendment, and that the same is true when the State lets it pass uncorrected, even if the lie goes only to the witness's credibility.
repere.source: Napue v. Illinois, 360 U.S. 264 (1959), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Chief Justice Warren

carte.punch: The witness denies any promise. The prosecutor knows that is false, and says nothing.
carte.idee: In the Napue case (Illinois), the key witness swears he was promised nothing, when the prosecutor had promised him a recommendation. The Supreme Court overturns the conviction in 1959: letting a known lie pass distorts a trial as much as provoking it.
carte.source_courte: Napue v. Illinois, U.S. Supreme Court, 1959

quiz.question: Why does the Court hold that the prosecutor's silence skews the trial, when the lie was not about the crime itself?
choix: Because the promise made to Hamer was forbidden by Illinois law
Because Hamer had also lied about being in the bar at the time of the shooting
Because a witness's truthfulness can decide guilt, and the jury did not know one of his reasons for testifying
Because a prosecutor who lets a lie pass is himself committing perjury before the jury
quiz.explication: The Court writes that a jury may base its decision on a witness's reliability, and that, informed of the promise, it might have concluded that Hamer was seeking the prosecutor's favor. It says nothing about the promise being prohibited, about another lie by Hamer, or about perjury by the prosecutor: it is the silence about the promise that skews the trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What sentence does Hamer receive for his own part in the August 21, 1938 shooting?
choix: The death penalty, like his accomplice Poe, who is executed
199 years in prison, after pleading guilty to the officer's murder
A fine and probation, in exchange for his testimony
Acquittal, the jury finding that he had not fired
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hamer pleads guilty to the officer's murder and receives 199 years in prison, the same sentence Napue will later receive; it is his accomplice Poe, not he, who is sentenced to death and executed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the existence of the promise made to Hamer revealed, later on?
choix: He testifies before the jury at Napue's second trial
He publishes an open letter in the Chicago press
He files a petition on Hamer's behalf in which he admits the promise
He confides it to a journalist, who investigates the case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Later, the former assistant prosecutor files a petition on Hamer's behalf and writes in it that he had indeed promised him a recommendation, and not through testimony, a letter in the press or a confidence to a journalist.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Illinois Supreme Court hold, before the case reaches the U.S. Supreme Court?
choix: It overturns the conviction and orders a new trial
It denies that the assistant prosecutor made a promise to Hamer
It holds Napue's appeal inadmissible without examining the merits
It acknowledges the promise and the lie, but refuses to overturn the conviction
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Illinois Supreme Court acknowledges that the promise existed and that the assistant prosecutor knew Hamer was lying, but it refuses to overturn the conviction, finding that the jury already knew a public defender was helping the witness.
